method: The modulation index is the peak frequency deviation divided by the highest modulating frequency, both in the same unit, so 75 kHz of deviation against a 15 kHz audio band gives an index of 5. Carson's rule puts the occupied bandwidth at twice the sum of the peak deviation and that top modulating frequency, because the carrier and its two nearest sideband groups spread one top frequency beyond the peak swing; 75 kHz and 15 kHz therefore give 180 kHz, which is why wideband FM broadcasting fits a 200 kHz channel. A single tone spreads its power over sidebands spaced by the modulating frequency whose amplitudes follow Bessel functions of the first kind with the index as argument; the page reports the usual rule-of-thumb count of index plus one strong sideband pairs and the span those pairs cover, labelled an estimate rather than a computed spectrum. Narrowband FM is reported at an index of 0.3 or less. Channel margin is the spacing minus the Carson bandwidth, and a negative margin is shown as bandwidth over the channel. The largest peak deviation that still fits is half the channel spacing minus the top modulating frequency, and none is reported when the audio band alone already fills half the channel. Peak deviation accepts 0.1 to 1000 kHz, the highest modulating frequency 0.05 to 100 kHz and channel spacing 1 to 2000 kHz, in ordinary decimal notation only; a missing, non-numeric or out-of-range value is rejected with an actionable message rather than defaulted. Channel fit uses the full spacing with no guard band, and stereo pilot injection, pre-emphasis, splatter filters, adjacent-channel protection ratios and the 99 percent occupancy definition of any particular radio service are not modelled. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Carson's bandwidth rule: an FM signal occupies about twice the sum of its peak frequency deviation and its highest modulating frequency

Angle modulation: the modulation index is the peak deviation divided by the modulating frequency, and a single-tone spectrum spreads into sidebands spaced by the modulating frequency whose amplitudes are Bessel functions of the index
Narrowband FM convention: an index of 0.3 or less leaves little power outside the carrier and first sideband pair
